title: Playing Backwater Blues at the school assembly
summary: Pushed by the music teacher to play at a school assembly, he played Bessie Smith's Backwater Blues; students cheered but teachers and the principal disapproved.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Something you heard. And then in the meantime, you'd be playing these records, you know, playing the records and things like that. And so now I'm getting on up there about 13 or 14 years old, you see, so by 13, 14, this fellow that took over the music department in the school, he came in the room one day and I was sitting down playing and he heard me playing and he says, "Look, I want you to play at the --" What was that they used to have? You know, they'd have, where everybody would go to the auditorium?
It wasn't commencement. They used to call it --
Yeah, where everybody goes to the auditorium and maybe the principal -- they used to call it sort of a pep meeting, you know.
When you all went there in the morning, do you mean?
No, like all the classes would come to the auditorium and --

Not everyday, no. Maybe this was just once every two weeks or something like that and like they would have a little pep meeting or something, they would call it. The principal might talk about something or somebody else talk about something and then they might have somebody to sing something. But he wanted me to play. And I says, "I can't play. I don't play. I can't play up there." So he says, "Just do what you did," and I didn't want to and I begged out of it. But I'll tell you what happened.

He called on me anyhow. So he called on me anyhow. So I went on up and the only thing that I knew was that thing that I had heart Bessie Smith do, you know, which was backwater blues, you know? And I just started playing that and the kids in school screamed and you know how they do and clapped their hands and screamed. And the next day in school, I caught it from everybody. The teacher was talking about me in my class. She says, "I think it was a shame a member of our class got up

there and played what he played," and the principal, everybody. "I'll never play anything." So I said -- so I didn't fool with no music. You know, I felt so bad. So I wouldn't play at the school no more. They come back and try to get me to play, you know?
I take it that these sort of church and sort of school people thought blues was too lowdown or something.
That's what they thought, yes. That's what they thought. And so consequently --
You wouldn't have thought your school pals would have thought that though, would you?

The school kids? Oh, the school kids, they loved it, the kids. Because they all had a ball, you know, they went to clapping and that's the reaction that I think turned the teachers and the principal and everybody --
It was the teachers that didn't like it.

Yes. But the music teacher told me, he said, "Listen, I don't care what they say, listen. Don't pay that no mind." So I told him, I says, "Everybody in every class I go to, they got me sitting up there feeling bad and like I've done something real bad or something, know what I mean?" And even one of my cousins come by our house one night. He said, "Well, I heard J.C. got up there in school and played the lowdown dirty blues."
